bp: A fact-checking pipeline starts before truth is judged. Someone first has to read a long document and decide which sentences or ideas are central enough to become checkable claims. That first step is easy to underestimate. A long article may contain background, opinions, quoted speech, side examples, hedged statements, and a few core factual assertions. Human fact-checkers know that not every factual sentence is worth extracting: a good claim should be important to the document, specific enough to test, and shaped in a way that later evidence can support or refute. The paper serves that bottleneck. Manual document-level extraction is expensive because it requires domain expertise, but automatic extraction can miss the human standard of quality. The proposed Human Value-Aligned approach tries to move expert judgment into zero-shot claim extraction, meaning the language model is asked to do the task without training on many new labeled examples for this exact setting.
wh: The hard part is that claim quality is not just grammatical correctness or topical relevance. A machine can pull out a sentence that looks factual but is too broad, too minor, too vague, or not central to the document's argument. Human fact-checkers judge several dimensions at once: whether the extracted claim captures the main point, whether it can be checked, whether it preserves the document's meaning, and whether it is useful for later verification. Those dimensions can conflict. A very short claim may be easy to compare with evidence but may lose context. A broad claim may sound central but be too loose to verify. The abstract says existing extraction and evaluation methods overlook critical dimensions that human fact-checkers consider essential. That creates a measurement problem as much as a generation problem: if the evaluator rewards the wrong notion of quality, the extractor learns or is prompted toward the wrong behavior.
naive: A smart beginner would ask a language model to summarize the document into a few factual claims, then compare those claims to expert-written claims using a text overlap score. That fails in two ways. First, summarization is not the same as fact-checkable claim selection: a summary may preserve the general story while omitting the precise assertions a fact-checker would inspect. Second, surface overlap can reward similar wording even when the extracted claim is not central, verifiable, or properly scoped. Another simple approach is to write a checklist by hand, but the paper's premise is that expert preferences must be elicited from annotations because the important dimensions are structured and task-specific. The naive method treats claim extraction as text shortening; the paper treats it as expert-valued selection.
ap: The core move is to make expert preferences explicit before asking the model to extract claims. The authors first elicit a structured set of Human Value Alignment dimensions from expert annotations. In plain terms, they look at expert judgments to identify the qualities that make a claim worth extracting. Those dimensions are then built into the prompt, so the model is not merely told to find claims but is guided toward the kind of claims expert fact-checkers prefer. The paper also adds an automatic evaluator based on a language model. That evaluator scores extracted claims across the same human-value dimensions and compares them with expert-written claims. Finally, the authors introduce a multi-level agreement metric to check whether the automatic evaluator is reliable. The important design choice is symmetry: the values used to guide extraction are also used to judge extraction quality.
mech: The mechanism starts with a long document and expert annotations. The annotations are not used only as answer keys; they are used to reveal the dimensions experts care about when they mark a claim as high quality. Those dimensions become a structured description of the target: centrality, checkability, closeness to expert intent, and other quality axes supported by the paper's HVA setup, though the abstract does not list every dimension. Next, the system places those dimensions into prompt instructions for a large language model. The input is the document plus the value-aware instruction. The model transforms the document into extracted claims, attempting to keep the claims aligned with those expert-derived quality axes. A second model-based component then evaluates the output. Instead of returning only one overall score, it scores claims across the HVA dimensions and quantifies how closely they align with expert-written claims. The final step is reliability checking: the multi-level agreement metric compares automatic evaluator behavior with human judgments at more than one level, so reliability is not treated as a single vague correlation. The outputs are the extracted claims, dimension-level assessment scores, and agreement evidence showing whether the evaluator tracks expert judgment.
math: Several mathematical ideas are doing work here. The first is learning from examples, in the modest sense of extracting a reusable rule from expert annotations. The system is not just memorizing expert claims; it is using annotations to infer what properties experts repeatedly reward. The second idea is scoring. A score compresses a complex judgment into a number or ordered assessment, which is useful because many extracted claims must be compared. But compression is risky: one score can hide whether a claim failed because it was unimportant, unverifiable, or poorly matched to the document. That is why dimension-level scoring matters. It keeps several axes visible instead of forcing all quality into one opaque grade. The third idea is agreement measurement. Agreement asks whether two judges, here humans and the automatic evaluator, tend to make compatible judgments. The paper's multi-level agreement metric matters because evaluator trust is itself uncertain. If the automatic evaluator disagrees with experts, better extraction scores would be hollow. The central tradeoff is scale versus fidelity: automated prompting and evaluation make document-level claim extraction cheaper, but only if the expert-derived dimensions preserve the real professional judgment they are meant to replace.
dots: This paper belongs to the misinformation and trust branch of the repo because it repairs the first link in a fact-checking chain: deciding what claim should be checked. Neighboring fact-checking papers focus on later links, such as retrieving evidence, resolving conflicts between a model's internal knowledge and external evidence, decomposing complex claims into dependent subclaims, or writing fact-checking reports from gathered sources. This paper sits earlier: bad extraction poisons everything downstream because the verifier may accurately check the wrong or least important claim. It also connects to ranking, because central claims must be selected from many possible statements under limited human attention. It connects to similarity, because extracted claims are compared with expert-written claims, though the useful comparison must go beyond shared wording. It connects to learning from examples, because expert annotations are turned into reusable dimensions. The broader field pattern is alignment: model behavior is steered toward human professional values rather than only toward fluent text.
ww: The approach should improve over the naive version because it changes the target the model is trying to hit. A generic extraction prompt leaves the model to infer what kind of claim matters, and a general language model may prefer claims that are salient, smooth, or summary-like rather than claims that expert fact-checkers would actually verify. By naming the expert-derived dimensions inside the prompt, the system gives the model a more precise operating standard. The evaluator then reinforces the same standard at measurement time. This reduces a common failure where generation and evaluation point in different directions: one component asks for useful claims while the metric rewards wording overlap. Dimension-level assessment also helps diagnose errors. If an extracted claim scores poorly on verifiability but well on centrality, the system and the human reader learn what went wrong. The reliability metric is important for the same reason. It asks whether the automatic judge deserves authority by checking its agreement with human judgments, rather than assuming a model-based evaluator is correct because it produces confident scores.
po: The payoff is a more scalable front end for automated fact-checking. Instead of requiring experts to read every long document and manually pull out central claims, the system can ask a language model to extract claims under expert-derived guidance. The abstract reports improved document-level claim extraction, with state-of-the-art chrF and P@N scores, and says the HVA evaluator reaches high agreement with human judgments. The practical gain is not only higher scores. It is a richer evaluation surface: fact-checkers can see dimension-level assessments of extracted claims, which makes failures more interpretable than a single pass-or-fail number. That helps turn automatic extraction into a tool that can be inspected, not merely trusted.
limits: The method depends on the expert annotations being broad and representative enough to define Human Value Alignment dimensions for future documents. If the experts share a narrow domain, language, or editorial style, the prompts may encode that narrowness as if it were universal claim quality. The abstract is cut off before all details are visible, so it does not prove which dimensions were used, how many experts contributed, or how the system behaves on adversarial, highly technical, or politically loaded documents. The evaluator is also a model-based judge, so its high agreement with humans must hold outside the tested data. Strong chrF and P@N scores show useful extraction performance, but they do not by themselves prove downstream fact-checking accuracy.
